Today
💧 Water 0 / 128 oz
  • Even mild dehydration (around 2% of body weight in fluid loss) can measurably reduce strength, endurance, and focus mid-session.
  • Thirst lags behind actual need, especially during hard training — drinking on a rough schedule works better than waiting to feel thirsty.
  • Pale yellow urine is a simple, reliable sign of good hydration; noticeably dark yellow usually means it's time to drink more.
  • Water helps regulate body temperature and lubricate joints during exercise — both directly affect how a session actually feels.
  • Replacing fluids after a hard or hot session helps kick off recovery — sweat losses add up fast in heat or humidity.
  • Coffee and alcohol don't reliably count toward hydration for everyone — for some people they have a mild diuretic effect.

Sleep
😴 No entries yet — log last night's sleep.
  • Adults generally need 7-9 hours a night (National Sleep Foundation / AASM); people training hard regularly often do better toward the top of that range, and some research on athletes points to 8-10 hours as the more accurate target during heavy training blocks.
  • Growth hormone release and muscle protein synthesis both ramp up during deep sleep — cutting sleep short doesn't just make you tired, it directly blunts the recovery you trained for.
  • Chronic short sleep (5-6 hours a night for several nights running) has been shown to reduce muscle protein synthesis by close to 20% — a bigger hit than most people expect from "just" losing sleep.
  • A full sleep cycle runs about 90 minutes; 5 cycles (~7.5 hrs) is a common target for waking up between cycles instead of mid-cycle, which often feels less groggy than the raw hour count alone would suggest.
  • Short sleep is linked to measurably higher injury risk during training, not just worse performance — this isn't only a recovery-quality issue.
  • A cool, dark room and cutting caffeine well before bed are the two most consistently supported sleep-hygiene habits — simple, unglamorous, and well-evidenced.

Blood Pressure Trend
Systolic (top number) charted below — the AHA categories weigh whichever of the two numbers is higher, so a normal-looking systolic trend doesn't rule out a diastolic issue on its own.
Blood Glucose Trend
Daily average across however many readings you logged that day, fasting and post-meal mixed together — a rough overall trend, not a substitute for reading each entry against its own context.
Meal Timing
Looks at days where you logged a meal shortly after training and a post-meal glucose reading after that — purely a readout of what you actually logged, not a claim about cause and effect. Needs meal times and post-meal glucose logged on the same days to show anything.

This isn't a diagnosis. This tool can't examine you, so it can't tell you what's actually injured or how long it'll take to heal — a doctor or physical therapist can. What it can do: keep a record of what happened (useful to bring to an appointment), flag symptoms that need prompt medical attention, and quiet down exercises that might aggravate the area while you get it checked out.

Get Form Feedback
Coaching from the Strength & Size knowledge base, since that's your active training style. Record a full working set, up to 60 seconds, from the side or a 3/4 angle — the coach reads frames across the whole set and can tell you whether your form holds up or breaks down as it goes, not just a single moment. Longer or larger clips are exactly where video reading tends to fail on iPhone, so 60 seconds is a real ceiling, not a suggestion.
🔒 Your clip goes directly from this device to Anthropic using your own API key — never through any other server. Only the written feedback below gets saved; the video itself is never stored, here or anywhere else.
